title: Word Embeddings
summary: How word2vec and GloVe turned words into dense semantic vectors — and the limitation that motivated contextual models.

slides.subTitle: A word is known by the company it keeps
slides.markdown: The whole field of embeddings rests on one linguistic idea: **words that appear in similar contexts tend to have similar meaning**. "Dog" and "cat" both show up near "vet", "leash", "pet" — so a model that learns to predict context from words (or vice versa) ends up placing "dog" and "cat" near each other in vector space, purely from co-occurrence statistics, with no dictionary or hand-labeling involved. This is why embeddings are called **learned**, not designed: the geometry falls out of how words are actually used across a huge text corpus.

slides.subTitle: CBOW vs skip-gram
slides.markdown: **word2vec** trains a shallow neural network on a proxy task, then throws the task away and keeps the learned weights as embeddings. Two variants: **CBOW** (continuous bag-of-words) predicts the center word from its surrounding context words; **skip-gram** does the reverse — predicts the surrounding context from the center word. Skip-gram tends to work better on rare words (it generates more training pairs per occurrence), while CBOW trains faster and does slightly better on frequent words. Neither variant is ever used for the prediction task itself in production — the trained weight matrix *is* the product.

slides.subTitle: Similar words cluster together
slides.markdown:
Once trained, each word is a point in a (typically 100–300 dimension) vector space, and geometric distance approximates semantic distance. Words used in similar contexts land close together; unrelated words land far apart. This is what makes embeddings useful downstream — a classifier can generalize from "good" to "great" because they're nearby vectors, something a raw one-hot or BoW representation could never offer.

slides.subTitle: king − man + woman ≈ queen
slides.markdown: The famous demo — vector("king") − vector("man") + vector("woman") lands near vector("queen") — shows embeddings capture **linear relational structure**, not just similarity clusters. The "man → woman" direction encodes something like a gender relationship, and that same offset applies consistently across many word pairs (king/queen, actor/actress). What it actually reveals: embeddings encode relationships as consistent vector arithmetic, which is a much stronger claim than "similar words are near each other" — it's what let embeddings power analogy tasks and word-relationship benchmarks, not just similarity search.

slides.subTitle: Global co-occurrence vs local context windows
slides.markdown:
word2vec learns purely from local context windows (a few words on either side); **GloVe** (Global Vectors) instead builds a global word-word co-occurrence matrix across the entire corpus first, then factorizes it to produce embeddings that directly optimize for reproducing those co-occurrence ratios.

| | word2vec | GloVe |
|---|---|---|
| Signal | Local context windows | Global co-occurrence counts |
| Training | Predictive (neural, online) | Count-based, then matrix factorization |
| Captures | Local syntactic + some semantic | Strong on global semantic/analogy structure |

In practice the two produce embeddings of similar quality; the choice mattered more for training infrastructure than for downstream accuracy, and both were largely superseded by contextual embeddings.

slides.subTitle: One fixed vector can't cover multiple meanings
slides.markdown: A common mistake is assuming embeddings "understand" a word. In reality, word2vec and GloVe assign **exactly one vector per word type**, regardless of context. "Bank" gets a single vector that has to average the meanings of a river bank and a financial institution — usually landing somewhere between them, well-suited to neither. Any sentence using "bank" gets the identical vector whether it's about kayaking or mortgages. This is a **structural** limitation, not a training bug — no amount of more data fixes it, because the model architecture only has room for one vector per word.

slides.subTitle: A preview of what transformers fix
slides.markdown:
| | Static embeddings (word2vec/GloVe) | Contextual embeddings (BERT/GPT-style) |
|---|---|---|
| Vectors per word | One, fixed at training time | Different vector per occurrence, computed at inference |
| Handles polysemy | No | Yes |
| Compute cost | Cheap lookup table | Full forward pass through a Transformer |

Contextual models compute a word's vector *on the fly* from its actual surrounding sentence, so "bank" in "river bank" and "bank" in "bank loan" get different vectors. That flexibility is exactly what the next generation of models — covered under attention and Transformers — was built to provide.

slides.subTitle: fastText's character n-gram embeddings
slides.markdown:
word2vec and GloVe both fail completely on a word never seen in training — there's simply no vector for it. **fastText** fixes this by representing each word as the **sum of its character n-gram vectors** (e.g. "where" contributes n-grams like "wh", "whe", "her", "ere", plus the whole word itself), and learning embeddings for those n-grams instead of, or in addition to, whole words.

A genuinely unseen word still has an embedding at inference time — it's built from n-gram pieces that likely appeared inside other training words — and this also helps morphologically related words ("run", "running", "runner") share structure through their overlapping character n-grams, something word-level word2vec can't do at all.

slides.subTitle: Embeddings inherit the biases of their training corpus
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Embeddings are learned purely from statistics, so they're neutral and free of human bias."

**Why it's wrong:** the distributional hypothesis that makes embeddings work (s01) is a double-edged sword — if a training corpus disproportionately associates "doctor" with male pronouns and "nurse" with female ones, the learned vectors encode that association as geometric structure, the same way they encode "dog" near "cat." The famous king−man+woman≈queen analogy generalizes to far less benign directions, like doctor−man+woman landing suspiciously close to nurse in embeddings trained on unfiltered web text.

**Correct model:** embeddings are a faithful mirror of the statistics in their training data, biases included — using them in a hiring, lending, or moderation system without auditing for and mitigating this (debiasing techniques, balanced training data, downstream fairness evaluation) risks encoding real-world discrimination directly into the model's geometry.
